outcome: I can build a chain of reasoning step by step, spot the weak link in someone else's chain, and choose evaluation points and conclusions that are supported.

learn.text:
Exam answers earn marks for **reasoning**, not just facts. Think of each answer as a bridge across a river.

**Build it.** Start from the event and show every link: *this causes that, so this happens*. Use linking words such as *so*, *because* and *this means that*. Do not jump straight to the answer.

**Break it.** Check each plank. Common cracks: the wrong curve shifts, a shift is confused with a **[[movement along the curve]]**, a step goes the wrong way (an inferior good, a complement), or a link is missing.

**Judge it.** For AO3 questions, weigh up what you found. Strong evaluation uses an economic idea: **[[price elasticity of demand]]**, **[[stakeholders]]**, the short run and the long run, **[[opportunity cost]]**, or the assumptions behind the theory. Then end with a **conclusion that is supported** by your arguments.
learn.caption: A chain of reasoning: build the links in order, then judge how far the answer holds.

try.goal: Build bridges of reasoning. In Level 1, place 19 of 24 planks right first time to earn the **Bridge Builder** stamp.
try.intro:
Good exam answers are chains: each step follows from the one before, like planks across a river.

Level 1 (**Build it**): tap the planks in order, from the event on the left bank to the answer on the right. Level 2 (**Break it**): one plank in each bridge is cracked. Find it, then choose the plank that fixes it. Level 3 (**Judge it**): the bridge is built. Choose the strongest evaluation point, then the best supported conclusion.

levels.title: Build it
levels.blurb: Put 6 chains of reasoning in order. Place 19 of 24 planks right first time.

levels.title: Break it
levels.blurb: Find and fix the cracked plank in 8 bridges. Score 13 of 16 first-try points.

levels.title: Judge it
levels.blurb: Choose the best evaluation and conclusion for 6 claims. Score 10 of 12 first-try points.

builds.event: A frost destroys much of the coffee harvest.
builds.question: What happens to the price and quantity of coffee?
planks: The supply of coffee decreases: the supply curve shifts left.
At the old price, quantity demanded is bigger than quantity supplied: a shortage.
Buyers compete for the coffee, so the price rises.
As the price rises, buyers demand less: a movement along the demand curve.
A new equilibrium: a higher price and a lower quantity.

builds.event: The government puts a specific tax on cigarettes. Demand is price inelastic.
builds.question: Will the tax cut smoking by a lot?
planks: Firms' costs rise by the tax on each pack.
Supply shifts up (left) by the amount of the tax.
At the old price there is a shortage, so the price buyers pay rises.
Demand is price inelastic, so the quantity demanded falls only a little.
Smoking falls a little, and the government earns a lot of tax revenue.

builds.event: A country moves resources into new machines and training.
builds.question: What happens to its PPC, now and later?
planks: Resources move to making capital goods, so fewer consumer goods are made now.
The consumer goods given up are the opportunity cost of the investment.
The quantity and quality of the factors of production increase.
The PPC shifts outwards: growth in production possibilities.
In the future, the economy can produce more of both goods.

builds.event: Smoke from a factory harms people who live nearby.
builds.question: Why is this a market failure?
planks: The smoke is an external cost to third parties.
So the marginal social cost (MSC) is above the marginal private cost (MPC).
The factory produces where MPC = MPB, at the market quantity Qm.
Qm is more than the social optimum Q*, where MSC = MSB.
Too much is produced, so there is a welfare loss: a market failure.

builds.event: A café raises the price of its lattes. Demand is price elastic.
builds.question: What happens to the café's total revenue?
planks: The price of a latte rises by a certain percentage.
Demand is price elastic, so quantity demanded falls by a bigger percentage.
The fall in quantity outweighs the rise in price.
Total revenue (price × quantity) falls.
So the café should not raise its price if it wants more revenue.

builds.event: The government sets a maximum rent below the equilibrium rent.
builds.question: What happens in the market for flats?
planks: The rent is held below the equilibrium rent.
At this rent, landlords offer fewer flats, and more people want one.
Quantity demanded is bigger than quantity supplied: a shortage.
The flats must be shared out another way, such as waiting lists.
Some renters pay less, but others cannot find a flat at all.

breaks.event: Incomes rise. Cars are a normal good.
planks: Consumers have more income to spend.
Demand for cars increases: the demand curve shifts right.
Supply of cars shifts right to meet the new demand.
At the old price there is excess demand, so the price rises.
A new equilibrium with a higher price and a higher quantity.

fixes.text: Supply does not shift: firms move up along the supply curve as the price rises.
fixes.feedback: Yes. Income is a determinant of demand. Firms respond to the higher price by moving along supply.

fixes.text: Demand shifts left, because cars now cost more.
fixes.feedback: A higher price never shifts demand. And higher incomes raise demand for a normal good.

fixes.text: The price falls to clear the extra demand.
fixes.feedback: Excess demand pushes the price up, not down.

breaks.why: The cracked plank shifted **supply**. Nothing changed firms' costs. They supply more because the price rose: a **movement along** supply.

breaks.event: The government subsidises solar panel producers.
planks: The government pays producers for each panel made.
Firms' costs fall, so supply shifts down (right).
The price rises because more panels are made.
Quantity demanded rises: a movement along demand.
More panels are sold, at a lower price.

fixes.text: At the old price there is excess supply, so the price falls.
fixes.feedback: Yes. More is supplied at every price, so the price falls to clear the market.

fixes.text: Demand shifts right because the government pays.
fixes.feedback: The subsidy goes to producers. It shifts supply, not demand.

fixes.text: The price stays the same because the subsidy goes to firms.
fixes.feedback: The extra supply pushes the price down. Buyers gain part of the subsidy.

breaks.why: When supply increases, the price **falls**. The cracked plank said it rises.

breaks.event: A bus company raises fares by 10%. Demand is price inelastic.
planks: Fares rise by 10%.
The number of passengers falls by 20%.
The rise in price outweighs the fall in quantity.
Total revenue rises.
So the company earns more from fares.

fixes.text: The number of passengers falls by less than 10%, for example 4%.
fixes.feedback: Yes. Price inelastic means quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price.

fixes.text: The number of passengers rises, because buses are a necessity.
fixes.feedback: By the law of demand, a higher fare still lowers the quantity demanded. Inelastic means it falls only a little.

fixes.text: The number of passengers stays exactly the same.
fixes.feedback: That would be perfectly inelastic. Price inelastic demand still falls, by a smaller percentage.

breaks.why: A 20% fall after a 10% rise means PED = −2: **elastic**. With inelastic demand, quantity falls by **less** than 10%.

breaks.event: The government sets a minimum wage above the equilibrium wage.
planks: The minimum wage is set above the equilibrium wage.
Firms want to hire fewer workers at the higher wage.
More people want to work at the higher wage.
So there is a shortage of labour.
Some workers earn more, but others cannot find a job.

fixes.text: The quantity of labour supplied is bigger than the quantity demanded: unemployment.
fixes.feedback: Yes. A wage above equilibrium causes excess supply of labour.

fixes.text: So the wage falls back to the equilibrium.
fixes.feedback: The minimum wage is the law. The wage cannot fall below it.

fixes.text: So demand for labour shifts right.
fixes.feedback: Nothing shifted demand. Firms move along their demand for labour.

breaks.why: Above equilibrium, more people want jobs than firms offer. That is **excess supply** of labour (unemployment), not a shortage.

planks: A streetlight lights the road for everyone who passes.
No one can be stopped from using it: it is non-excludable.
One person's use does not reduce what is left for others: it is non-rivalrous.
So everyone pays their fair share to a private firm.
The market does not provide it, so the government may.

fixes.text: So people can use it without paying: the free rider problem.
fixes.feedback: Yes. Firms cannot charge, so they will not supply it.

fixes.text: So the streetlight is a private good.
fixes.feedback: A private good is rivalrous and excludable. A streetlight is neither.

fixes.text: So the price of streetlights rises.
fixes.feedback: There is no market price here. Firms cannot charge for a non-excludable good.

breaks.why: Because no one can be excluded, people can **free ride**. That is why the market will not provide it.

breaks.event: Education gives benefits to the people who study and to society.
planks: People who are educated earn more.
Society also gains: a more skilled workforce and better decisions.
So marginal social benefit is below marginal private benefit.
The market produces less than the social optimum.
There is underconsumption: a market failure.

fixes.text: So marginal social benefit is above marginal private benefit.
fixes.feedback: Yes. The external benefit is added to the private benefit.

fixes.text: So marginal social cost is above marginal private cost.
fixes.feedback: That is a negative production externality. Education gives a positive consumption externality.

fixes.text: So the market produces too much education.
fixes.feedback: With an external benefit, the market produces too little.

breaks.why: An external **benefit** puts MSB **above** MPB, so the market underprovides.

breaks.event: The price of printers falls a lot.
planks: Printers are cheaper, so more printers are bought.
Printers and ink are complements.
Demand for ink falls, because people spend their money on printers.
At the old price, there is excess demand for ink.
The price and quantity of ink rise.

fixes.text: Demand for ink increases: the demand curve for ink shifts right.
fixes.feedback: Yes. More printers means more people need ink.

fixes.text: Supply of ink shifts left.
fixes.feedback: The price of printers is a determinant of demand for ink, a complement.

fixes.text: There is a movement along the demand curve for ink.
fixes.feedback: The price of ink did not change first. A change in a complement's price shifts demand.

breaks.why: For **complements**, a lower price of one good **increases** demand for the other.

breaks.event: Many boats fish in the same sea.
planks: Fish in the sea are rivalrous: a fish caught by one boat cannot be caught by another.
No one can be stopped from fishing: they are non-excludable.
Each boat catches as many fish as it can.
The fish stock grows, because more boats take more care of it.
The stock collapses: the tragedy of the commons.

fixes.text: Fish are caught faster than they can breed, so the stock falls.
fixes.feedback: Yes. That is the link to the collapse.

fixes.text: The price of fish falls to zero.
fixes.feedback: That does not follow. The problem is the stock running down.

fixes.text: The government owns all the fish, so nothing changes.
fixes.feedback: No one owns a common pool resource. That is part of the problem.

breaks.why: When each boat takes as much as it can, fish are caught **faster than they breed**, so the stock falls.

judges.claim: A tax on sugary drinks will greatly reduce how many people drink them.
judges.analysis: The tax shifts supply up. The price of sugary drinks rises and the quantity falls.

evals.text: Demand for sugary drinks may be price inelastic, because of habit, so consumption may fall only a little.
evals.feedback: Yes. It questions how big the effect is, using PED.

evals.text: The tax shifts supply up, so the price rises and the quantity falls.
evals.feedback: That repeats the analysis. Evaluation asks how far it is true.

evals.text: Sugary drinks are unhealthy, so people should stop drinking them.
evals.feedback: That is an opinion. It does not weigh up the tax.

conclusions.text: The tax will cut consumption, but by how much depends on PED. It may work best with campaigns that inform people.
conclusions.feedback: Yes. A supported judgement that uses the evaluation.

conclusions.text: The tax will stop everyone drinking sugary drinks.
conclusions.feedback: Too strong. Your evaluation showed demand may be inelastic.

conclusions.text: The tax is unfair, so it should never be used.
conclusions.feedback: That judgement ignores the analysis and gives no evidence.

judges.claim: A maximum price on bread helps low-income families.
judges.analysis: The maximum price is below equilibrium, so bread is cheaper, but quantity demanded is bigger than quantity supplied.

evals.text: Families who can buy bread gain, but the shortage means some cannot buy any, and a black market may appear.
evals.feedback: Yes. It weighs who gains against who loses.

evals.text: The maximum price is set below the equilibrium price.
Bread should be free for everyone.
evals.feedback: That is an opinion, not an evaluation of the policy.

conclusions.text: It helps the families who get bread, but the shortage harms others. A subsidy or cash transfers may help without a shortage.
conclusions.feedback: Yes. It judges the policy and compares an alternative.

conclusions.text: It helps every family, because the price is lower.
conclusions.feedback: That ignores the shortage you found.

conclusions.text: Bread is not important to families.
conclusions.feedback: That has nothing to do with the analysis.

judges.claim: A higher minimum wage helps low-paid workers.
judges.analysis: The minimum wage is above the equilibrium wage, so workers who have jobs earn more, but the quantity of labour demanded falls.

evals.text: Workers who keep their jobs gain, but some may lose their jobs. The size of the job loss depends on how much firms cut hiring.
evals.feedback: Yes. It weighs gainers against losers and says what it depends on.

evals.text: The minimum wage is above the equilibrium wage.

evals.feedback: That is a value judgement with no economic reasoning.

conclusions.text: It helps workers who keep their jobs, but it may cause some unemployment. The harm is smaller if firms do not cut many jobs.
conclusions.feedback: Yes. Balanced, and it says when the policy works best.

conclusions.text: It always causes mass unemployment, so it never helps.
conclusions.feedback: Too strong. Your evaluation said it depends on how much firms cut hiring.

conclusions.text: Minimum wages are popular, so they work.
conclusions.feedback: Popularity is not evidence that a policy works.

judges.claim: A carbon tax will fix pollution from power stations.
judges.analysis: The tax raises the private cost of producing electricity towards the social cost, so output falls towards Q*.

evals.text: It is hard to measure the external cost, so the tax may be set too low or too high. In the short run, firms may have no cleaner option.
evals.feedback: Yes. It looks at a key assumption and at short run versus long run.

evals.text: The tax raises the private cost towards the social cost.

evals.feedback: True, but it does not weigh up the tax.

conclusions.text: It can move output towards Q*, but how well depends on setting the right tax and on cleaner options in the long run.
It will remove all pollution at once.
conclusions.feedback: Too strong. Output falls towards Q*, and Q* is not zero.

conclusions.text: Taxes are always bad for the economy.
conclusions.feedback: A sweeping claim with no support.

judges.claim: A subsidy for electric cars is the best way to cut emissions from cars.
judges.analysis: The subsidy shifts the supply of electric cars down, so their price falls and more are sold.

evals.text: It has an opportunity cost: the money could fund public transport, which might cut more emissions for each dollar.
evals.feedback: Yes. Best way means comparing it with other uses of the money.

evals.text: The subsidy shifts supply down, so more electric cars are sold.

evals.feedback: That is not about emissions or the policy.

conclusions.text: It raises electric car sales, but whether it is the best way depends on its cost compared with policies such as public transport.
conclusions.feedback: Yes. It answers "best way" by comparing.

conclusions.text: It is the best way, because more electric cars are sold.
conclusions.feedback: More sales does not show it is the best way. Compare the alternatives.
Too strong, and it ignores your analysis.

judges.claim: Putting fruit at eye level in the school cafeteria will make students eat healthily. (HL)
judges.analysis: This is a nudge: the choice architecture changes, but every option is still there.

evals.text: It keeps freedom of choice and costs little, but the effect may be small and may fade over time.
evals.feedback: Yes. Strengths and limitations of the nudge.

evals.text: Fruit at eye level is a nudge.

evals.feedback: That is an opinion about taste, not an evaluation.

conclusions.text: It is a cheap way to nudge students towards fruit, but it works best alongside other policies, such as education about diet.
conclusions.feedback: Yes. A supported judgement with a sensible next step.

conclusions.text: It will make every student eat healthily.
conclusions.feedback: Too strong. Nudges change some choices, not all.
That does not follow from the analysis.

check.prompt: What makes a **chain of reasoning** strong?

options.text: Each step follows from the one before, with no jumps.
options.feedback: Yes. Every link is shown, so the reader can follow it.

options.text: It uses as many key terms as possible.
options.feedback: Key terms help, but only if each step links to the next.

options.text: It jumps straight from the event to the answer.
options.feedback: That skips the links. Examiners reward the steps in between.

options.text: It is as long as possible.
options.feedback: Length does not make it strong. Clear links do.

hints: Think of a bridge: what happens if a plank is missing?
Can the reader see why each step happens?
check.worked: Example: frost → supply falls (shifts left) → shortage at the old price → price rises → new equilibrium with higher price, lower quantity.
check.explanation: A strong chain shows **every link**: each step is caused by the one before.

check.prompt: Incomes rise. Holidays abroad are a normal good. So the price of holidays rises. **Which link is missing?**

options.text: Demand for holidays increases: the demand curve shifts right.
options.feedback: Yes. That is the link between higher income and a higher price.

options.text: Supply of holidays increases.
options.feedback: Income is a determinant of demand. And more supply would lower the price.

options.text: Holidays become an inferior good.
options.feedback: Holidays are a normal good here: demand rises with income.

options.text: The price of flights falls.
options.feedback: That is a different event. It is not the missing link.

hints: Is income a determinant of demand or supply?
What must happen before the price can rise?
check.worked: Example: a fashion makes trainers popular → demand for trainers increases → excess demand at the old price → price rises.
check.explanation: Higher income → **demand for a normal good increases** → excess demand at the old price → the price rises.

check.prompt: Find the **cracked plank**: "(1) Incomes fall. (2) Bus travel is an inferior good. (3) So demand for bus travel falls. (4) So fewer people take the bus."

options.text: Plank 3: demand for an inferior good rises when incomes fall.
options.feedback: Yes. For an inferior good, demand moves the opposite way to income.

options.text: Plank 1: incomes cannot fall.
options.feedback: Incomes can fall, for example in a recession.

options.text: Plank 2: bus travel is always a normal good.
options.feedback: Bus travel is a common example of an inferior good.

options.text: Plank 4: it should say more people walk.
options.feedback: Plank 4 follows from plank 3. The crack is earlier.

hints: When income falls, what happens to demand for an inferior good?
check.worked: Example: incomes fall and people buy more store-brand food (inferior good) and fewer restaurant meals (normal good).
check.explanation: For an **inferior good**, demand **rises** when incomes fall. So plank 3 is cracked.

options.text: However, demand for petrol is price inelastic, so the tax may cut driving only a little.
options.feedback: Yes. It weighs how well the policy works.

options.text: The tax shifts the supply of petrol up.
options.feedback: That is analysis: what happens.

options.text: Petrol is a fuel used by cars.
options.feedback: That is a fact, not evaluation.

options.text: The price of petrol rises from P₁ to P₂.
options.feedback: That is analysis from the diagram.

hints: Evaluation weighs up strengths and limitations.
Look for a sentence that questions how far something works.
check.worked: Example: "However, in the long run drivers may switch to electric cars, so the tax works better over time."
check.explanation: **Evaluation** weighs up: it asks how far, for whom, and when something works.

check.prompt: A government subsidises bus fares. Which is the **strongest** evaluation point?

options.text: The subsidy has an opportunity cost: the money could have been spent on schools or health care.
options.feedback: Yes. It weighs the policy against what is given up.

options.text: The subsidy shifts the supply of bus travel down.
options.feedback: That is analysis, not evaluation.

options.text: Buses are good.
options.feedback: That is an opinion with no reasoning.

options.text: Bus fares are paid in money.
options.feedback: That is a fact, and not relevant to evaluation.

hints: Strong evaluation is specific and uses economic ideas.
What is given up to pay for the subsidy?
check.worked: Example: "A sugar tax raises revenue, but it takes a bigger share of low incomes, so it may be regressive."
check.explanation: Strong evaluation uses an **economic idea**, such as opportunity cost, PED, stakeholders, or short run versus long run.

check.prompt: Analysis showed a maximum price makes food cheaper but causes a shortage. Which conclusion is **best supported**?

options.text: It helps buyers who get the food, but the shortage harms others, so a subsidy may be a better way to help.
options.feedback: Yes. It uses the analysis and reaches a balanced judgement.

options.text: It helps everyone, because the price is lower.
options.feedback: That ignores the shortage.

options.text: Maximum prices are always wrong.
options.feedback: Too sweeping, and not supported by evidence.

options.text: Food is expensive.
options.feedback: That is not a conclusion about the policy.

hints: A good conclusion uses the arguments that came before.
Does it mention both the gain and the harm?
check.worked: Example: "The tax cuts consumption, but by how much depends on PED, so it works best with awareness campaigns."
check.explanation: A **supported conclusion** uses both sides of the evaluation and says when or how far something works.

check.prompt: Which phrase usually starts an **evaluation** point?

options.text: "However, this depends on..."
options.feedback: Yes. It signals that you are weighing up.

options.text: "The definition of..."
options.feedback: That starts a definition (AO1).

options.text: "The curve shifts to..."
options.feedback: That starts analysis.

options.text: "In the diagram, label..."
options.feedback: That is about drawing, not evaluation.

hints: Which phrase turns to the other side?
check.worked: Other evaluation starters: "On the other hand...", "In the long run...", "For some stakeholders...".
check.explanation: Phrases such as **"however"**, **"on the other hand"** and **"this depends on"** signal evaluation.

check.prompt: A frost destroys much of the coffee harvest. The flow chart shows the chain of reasoning. **Label it.** Choose what each box shows.

diagram.title: A flow chart of four empty boxes
diagram.description: Four empty boxes in a row, joined by arrows from left to right. Letter A is on the first box, B on the second, C on the third and D on the fourth.

slots.feedback: The frost cuts the harvest, so supply decreases first.
With less supplied at the old price, there is a shortage.
The shortage pushes the price up.
The new equilibrium has a higher price and a lower quantity.

hints: Who does a frost affect first: buyers or sellers?
What happens at the old price when supply falls?
check.worked: Example: a new technology → supply increases → surplus at the old price → price falls → lower price, higher quantity.
check.explanation: Frost → **supply decreases** → **shortage at the old price** → **the price rises** → **higher price, lower quantity**.

explain.prompt: Explain how a frost that destroys much of the coffee harvest affects the price of coffee. Then add one evaluation point.
explain.facts:
- A frost destroys much of the **coffee harvest**.
- Before the frost, the coffee market is in equilibrium.
- Demand for coffee is price inelastic, because many people drink it every day.

options.text: demand for coffee increases, because people want more coffee.
options.why: The frost affects growers, not how much people want coffee.

options.text: the supply of coffee decreases, so the supply curve shifts left.
options.why: Right. Less coffee can be supplied at every price.

options.text: the price of coffee falls, because there is less of it.
options.why: Less supply pushes the price up, not down.

options.text: quantity demanded is bigger than quantity supplied, so there is a shortage.
options.why: Right. That is the link to the price rise.

options.text: there is a surplus, because buyers want less.
options.why: Buyers' wants did not change. Supply fell, so there is a shortage.

options.text: the market stays in equilibrium.
options.why: Supply has fallen, so the old price no longer clears the market.

options.text: the price falls until the surplus is gone.
options.why: There is a shortage, not a surplus.

options.text: demand shifts left to match supply.
options.why: Demand does not shift. Buyers move along demand as the price rises.

options.text: the price rises until a new equilibrium is reached, with a higher price and a lower quantity.
because demand for coffee is price inelastic, the price may rise a lot while the quantity falls only a little.
options.why: Right. It uses PED to judge the size of the effect.

options.text: coffee is a popular drink.
options.why: That is a fact. It does not weigh anything up.

options.text: the supply curve shifts left.

explain.own: Add your own sentence about a stakeholder who gains or loses, such as coffee farmers whose crops survived.

teacherNotes: Build, Break, Judge practises the chain of reasoning behind AO2 answers and the evaluation behind AO3 answers, using content from 1.1 and 2.1 to 2.9 (one Judge it case is HL). Level 1 works well as a whole-class warm-up: read the event and ask students to call out the first plank. In Level 2, ask students why each cracked plank is tempting: these are the most common slips in Paper 1 answers. In Level 3, point out that the wrong evaluation options either repeat the analysis or give an unsupported opinion.
